title: Toulouse to Dornachbrugg: the Tutor, the Battle, and the Source of the Grail
years: c. 755-848 (Greub's redating; conventional chronicles close the life in 812 or 814)
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Ward of Aquitaine: Autun to Toulouse

stops.name: Autun, born into the kin of the Carolingians
stops.campa: Thierry, count of Autun, and his wife Aldana bring a son into the world in the hill country of Burgundy, kin by blood to the house that will crown Charlemagne. The chroniclers give no day, only the century's turning decade. He is called Guilhem in the tongue of the south he will make his own, Willehalm in the tongue of the poets who will carry him three centuries forward as a name the whole Rhine and Rhone will recognize. Nothing yet marks him; the marches of Septimania and the towers of a grail he cannot imagine wait beyond the Pyrenees and the Vosges both.
suggested_refs: The Vita Sancti Willelmi, the twelfth-century hagiography compiled at Gellone

stops.name: Toulouse, ward and count: the boy-king's guardian
stops.campa: Charlemagne names Guilhem Count of Toulouse, the frontier post nearest the Andalusian marches, and sets him beside the child Louis, crowned sub-king of Aquitaine at three years old and now growing toward manhood inside walls the Saracens test every campaigning season. Guilhem drills the boy in arms and counsel both, the elder cousin standing where a father should. The Astronomer, who will one day write Louis's own life, remembers Guilhem's name among the magnates who raised the prince who will become emperor. Neither of them yet knows how long the debt of this schoolroom will run.
suggested_refs: The Vita Hludowici Imperatoris (the Astronomer), on Louis's Aquitanian upbringing

segments.name: The Marches of Septimania: Orbieu and Barcelona

stops.name: The Orbieu, the field lost and the march held
stops.campa: Hisham I's army sweeps into Septimania in the campaigning season, and Guilhem meets them on the banks of the Orbieu below Narbonne. The field goes against him: the annals record a Frankish rout, kinsmen and vassals cut down around him, the count himself barely escaping the press. But the invaders, bled white by the stand, turn back toward Barcelona rather than press on to Toulouse or Narbonne. The marches hold because the price of breaking them was made too high on this one river's bank. Guilhem carries the defeat home and rebuilds the line through the winter.
suggested_refs: The Royal Frankish Annals, entry for 793
sources: Royal Frankish Annals (Annales regni Francorum), s.a. 793

stops.name: Narbonne, the muster of Aquitaine and Provence
stops.campa: For the siege the young king Louis is ordering against Barcelona, Guilhem gathers the levies of his own march: Franks, Goths, Provençals, Basques and Aquitanians mustering under Narbonne's walls before the long road south. He is the seasoned hand among the captains, the one who has already lost a field to this enemy and knows what the crossing of the passes will cost. The army that forms here will sit before Barcelona through the autumn and winter, starving the city rather than storming it, a patience Guilhem argues for out of his own hard lesson at the Orbieu.
suggested_refs: The chanson cycle's later memory of Guilhem as commander of the Barcelona host

stops.name: Barcelona, the city starved into surrender
stops.campa: After a siege of months the governor Sa'dun surrenders Barcelona to Louis and Guilhem without a final assault, the granaries exhausted before the walls are breached. Guilhem rides in among the first captains, the frontier he has bled for pushed at last past the Pyrenees into Spain itself. Ermold the Black will later set the whole campaign in verse for the emperor's court, naming Guilhem among the great of the army. It is the summit of his career as a count of the sword, and, though none present can know it, the last such summit the ordinary chronicles will fully credit to him.
suggested_refs: Ermoldus Nigellus, In Honorem Hludowici, book I, on the fall of Barcelona

segments.name: Gellone: the Monk's Turn and the Vanishing Terminus

stops.name: Gellone, the abbey founded in the desert gorge
stops.campa: In the wild gorge below Aniane, where the Verdus stream cuts through white stone, Guilhem founds a monastery and endows it with land and church plate, placing it under the rule of his friend Benedict of Aniane. Among the gifts he lays on the altar is a splinter of the True Cross, sent to him by his cousin Charlemagne. The place will take his own name after his death, Saint-Guilhem-le-Désert, the desert of Saint William, though on this day it is simply Gellone, a count's retreat built while the count is still very much a man of the world.
suggested_refs: The abbey church of Saint-Guilhem-le-Désert, still holding the relic of the True Cross

stops.name: Gellone, the cowl taken, the sword laid down
stops.campa: Two years after founding it, Guilhem resigns Toulouse and enters his own abbey as a monk, exchanging the count's mantle for the habit, carrying his own building stone up from the river with the other brothers, by the tradition's telling, so that no labor of the house is beneath him. Benedict of Aniane's strict rule governs the cloister; Guilhem submits to it as he once submitted to the discipline of the march. The warrior who broke at the Orbieu and stood at Barcelona now keeps silence, works the terraces, and waits on God the way he once waited on the Saracen advance.
suggested_refs: Benedict of Aniane's rule, kept at Gellone under Guilhem's obedience

stops.name: Gellone, the terminus the world's chronicles record
stops.campa: On this day, by the calendar every later martyrology and the Church itself will keep, the monk-count dies at Gellone and is buried before his own altar; some copies of the record push the date two years further, to 814, but all agree the story closes here. This is the terminus the ordinary chronicles give, and the terminus his own witness, Kyot, will later refuse. The world writes its epitaph and moves on into Louis's reign; the deeper current the poets will one day call Willehalm's own report runs past this stone unbroken, carrying the man another thirty-six years into events no chronicle here anticipates.
suggested_refs: The feast of Saint William of Gellone, kept 28 May since his 1066 canonization
sources: Werner Greub, Willehalm-Kyot: der Gewährsmann Wolframs von Eschenbach (1991)

stops.name: Oransche, Arabel won: the city and the bride
stops.campa: Between the wars the tradition sets the winning of Oransche: Willehalm takes the city on the Rhone from King Tybalt, and with it the queen Arabel, who leaves faith, crown, and husband to be baptized Gyburc and become his wife. The Glorieta tower becomes their house. Every grief that follows on the plain of Alischanz is already contained in this one wedding, for Tybalt's kin will cross the sea to take back the woman and the march both. The chansons will sing the taking of Orange for four centuries; Wolfram will hold the marriage up instead, love strong enough to answer for a war.
suggested_refs: La Prise d'Orange (chanson de geste), the winning of the city and of Orable-Guibourc

stops.name: Aachen, the pupil crowned, the tutor recalled
stops.campa: Louis, the boy Guilhem once schooled in the Toulouse garrison, now sits sole emperor at Aachen, his father three years in the grave. War gathers again in the south: King Tybalt's kin muster against the March of Provence, where Willehalm now holds the border and keeps, by the epic's account, a converted wife once named Arabel and now called Gyburc. Word runs north to the imperial court that the march is threatened. Louis remembers the man who raised him at Toulouse and marks him for the coming call, not knowing the summons will run through the oldest debt either of them carries.
suggested_refs: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Willehalm, on Willehalm's standing as March Count of Provence

stops.name: Alischanz, the first field, Vivianz slain
stops.campa: On the plain the poets call Alischanz, Willehalm's own host meets Tybalt's army and is broken. His young nephew Vivianz, sent ahead with the vanguard, fights to the last blade rather than yield and dies calling on God with his own hand pressed to his wound, a death the epic holds up for two centuries as the pattern of a Christian knight's end. Willehalm alone of the great captains rides clear of the slaughter, Gyburc's city of Oransche shut behind him with his wife inside it, and turns his horse north, not toward safety but toward Aachen and the debt owed him by an emperor he once carried on his own shoulder.
suggested_refs: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Willehalm, book II, the death of Vivianz

stops.name: Aachen, before the throne, the plea answered
stops.campa: Willehalm rides into Aachen still bloodied from the field, forces his way past the chamberlains, and stands before Louis to demand the relief he is owed, the epic sparing nothing of the emperor's hesitation or the old tutor's fury at finding gratitude so slow. Louis grants the host at last. It is, the poem insists on remembering, the pupil paying the debt of the schoolroom at Toulouse, arms instead of grammar, thirty years returned in a single audience. Willehalm rides south again at the head of a second, larger army, Gyburc still holding Oransche's walls against Tybalt's siege behind him.
suggested_refs: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Willehalm, book V, the audience at the imperial court

stops.name: Alischanz, the second field, Gyburc's toleration and the reckoning won
stops.campa: Before the second battle Gyburc herself counsels the Christian captains to spare the defeated rather than slaughter them, heathen or not, her own crossing from one faith to the other still raw enough to make her plead for the men on the other side of the field she was born into. Willehalm's relief host breaks Tybalt's siege and wins the field this time, avenging Vivianz and holding Oransche and the whole March of Provence. It is the last war Guilhem-Willehalm will fight; from this plain the road he takes turns east and north, away from the frontier he has spent his life defending, toward Alsace and a different kind of search.
suggested_refs: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Willehalm, book IX, Gyburc's speech for tolerance

segments.name: The Grail Quest: Toledo to Arlesheim

stops.name: Dôlet, the discarded manuscript of Flegetanis
stops.campa: With the march at peace, Willehalm-Kyot rides down through Spain to Toledo, the city of translators, and there, by Wolfram's own sworn account, finds the foundation of the whole adventure lying discarded, written in heathen letters. It is the starwriting of Flegetanis, the astronomer of Solomon's blood who read the name of the grail in the constellations and left it on the page for whoever could follow. Kyot has the Arabic learned in his years against the Saracens; he had to master that alphabet first, the poet says, without any art of black magic, and his baptism is what lets the writing yield.
stops.quote: Kyôt der meister wol bekant / ze Dôlet verworfen ligen vant / in heidenischer schrifte / dirre âventiure gestifte
suggested_refs: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, book IX, the Flegetanis passage

stops.name: Anschouwe, the chronicles searched, the grail-family found
stops.campa: Flegetanis's starwriting names the grail but not its keepers, so Kyot turns scholar in his old age and hunts the Latin chronicles of the lands for a people fit to guard it. He reads Britain and elsewhere, France and Ireland, and in Anjou he finds the tale at last: the line of Mazadan set down in a book, the genealogy that runs to Titurel and Frimutel and to Herzeloyde and her sisters. The search that will end on a hillside above Arlesheim begins here among parchments, an old soldier reading his way toward the family he does not yet know he will marry into.
stops.quote: er las der lande chrônicâ / ze Britâne unt anderswâ, / ze Francrîche unt in Yrlant: / ze Anschouwe er diu mære vant
suggested_refs: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, book IX, Kyot's search of the chronicles

stops.name: Andlau, the wayside altar and the search begun
stops.campa: Free of the border war for the first time in years, Willehalm turns north from Anjou toward the upper Rhine, following the starwriting's hint toward a vessel called the grail. At Andlau in the Alsatian hills he keeps vigil at a wayside shrine before the last leg of the search, a stop later tradition will remember when the counts of Andlau themselves take up the grail road as their own inheritance centuries on. He carries with him the captivity-won Arabic learning that first let him read Flegetanis's starwriting, the only western man, the tradition insists, equipped to recognize what he is about to find.
suggested_refs: The later Route du Gral association founded by the counts of Andlau, Strasbourg
sources: Ellen Schalk, 'Kyot and the Stellar Script of Parsifal' (1987)

stops.name: Arlesheim, the Hornikopf, Munsalvaesche found
stops.campa: On the wooded quarry-hill above Arlesheim, in a landscape the tradition later calls the terre de salvaesche, Willehalm finds the wooden grail-palace and its underground rock temple that Wolfram will name Munsalvaesche. He has followed Flegetanis's starwriting and his own years of searching to this one hillside on the edge of the Jura, and what he finds there answers both. The steel door at the temple's rear is said to yield only to one who already carries the story half-written in him. Willehalm-Kyot, soldier, monk, and now pilgrim, crosses that threshold as the last labor of a life that keeps refusing its own ending.
suggested_refs: The Hornikopf quarry above the Arlesheim Ermitage, proposed site of Munsalvaesche

stops.name: Arlesheim, the marriage to Schoysiane, the grail-bearer
stops.campa: Within Munsalvaesche's household Willehalm meets Schoysiane, sister of Herzeloyde and daughter of the grail king's line, the woman the tradition names grail-bearer for the office she keeps at the temple's threshold. He marries her there, an old soldier and monk taking up a third vocation he never sought as a boy in Toulouse. It is a brief marriage measured against the length of the life that surrounds it, but the tradition holds it as the hinge of everything that follows: through Schoysiane, Willehalm-Kyot becomes kin by blood to the grail family whose secret he had until now only read about in a captured Arabic book.
suggested_refs: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, on Schoysiane, sister of Herzeloyde

segments.name: Catalonia and the Loss of Schoysiane

stops.name: Katelangen, the dukedom and the household
stops.campa: Willehalm-Kyot brings his bride south again to Katelangen, the Catalan march he has held since the wars of his youth, now duke where he was once count, the frontier of his soldiering years become the seat of a different kind of life. Schoysiane keeps the household while he divides his time between the duties of the march and the grail-book he has begun, by the tradition's account, setting down in his own hand what Flegetanis wrote in the stars and what he has seen with his own eyes at Munsalvaesche. It is the shortest peace of his long life, and the tradition lets it stay unshadowed for less than two years.
suggested_refs: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, on Kyot of Katelangen

stops.name: Katelangen, Schoysiane's death, Sigune's birth
stops.campa: Schoysiane dies bearing their daughter, and the tradition gives the father no long grief to speak, only the fact set down plainly the way Kyot is said to set down every hard fact of his own life: the mother lost, the child, Sigune, living. Willehalm-Kyot names her and holds the newborn in a house built for a marriage that has already ended. He is past sixty by the ordinary count of his years, a widower twice over now in different registers, monk's cowl and count's mantle and grail-bearer's husband all laid down or taken up and set aside within a single decade.
suggested_refs: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, on Sigune's birth and Schoysiane's death

stops.name: Odilienberg, the infant Sigune given to Hohenburg
stops.campa: Willehalm-Kyot carries the infant Sigune north across the mountains to the Odilienberg, the holy height in Alsace where the nuns of Hohenburg keep the house Odile built two generations before, and gives the child into their fosterage rather than raise her alone on a war-worn march. From this height the whole Rhine plain opens below the convent walls, a healthier cradle by far than a dukedom bordered by raiding parties. He rides back to Katelangen without her, an old man handing the last thing his wife gave him to strangers in habits, trusting the mountain and its sisters the way he once trusted Benedict's rule at Gellone.
suggested_refs: Kloster Hohenburg on the Odilienberg, founded by Saint Odile

segments.name: The Long Silence at Le Verdus

stops.name: Le Verdus, the second retreat
stops.campa: Willehalm-Kyot returns a last time to the hunting lodge of Le Verdus in the gorge below Gellone, the stream that gives the valley its name running past walls he built himself as a young count. He does not re-enter the abbey's cloister this time, by the tradition's account, but keeps a hermit's house at Le Verdus, apart from the brothers yet within call of the bells he endowed. Here, in the years the ordinary chronicles have already closed his book, he works at the grail-narrative in earnest: Flegetanis's starwriting, the fall and rise of Alischanz, the marriage and the loss, folded into an account he tells no one is meant to outlast him.
suggested_refs: Le Verdus stream and gorge below Saint-Guilhem-le-Désert

stops.name: Le Verdus, word of Sigune and the leash of Schionatulander
stops.campa: Word reaches the old man at Le Verdus of his daughter, grown now at Hohenburg and betrothed to a young page named Schionatulander: the strange story of a leashed hound bolting into the forest trailing a leash inscribed with a story never finished, and the boy dying in a hunt undertaken to win it back for her. Willehalm-Kyot, who has buried a wife and given away an infant, receives the report the way he has learned to receive all grief now, as material for the account he is building rather than a wound to nurse alone. The unfinished leash-text will become, centuries later, Wolfram's own unfinished Titurel.
suggested_refs: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Titurel, the fragment of Sigune and Schionatulander

stops.name: Le Verdus, the brother Tampenteire's death and a second niece orphaned
stops.campa: News comes south that Willehalm-Kyot's brother Tampenteire has died, leaving a daughter, Condwiramurs, without a father's protection at the age when a great house's daughters are most exposed to the ambitions of neighbors. The old man at Le Verdus, who has already raised one motherless child by proxy through the nuns of Hohenburg, takes up the office again for his brother's line. He sends word north that he will come himself rather than trust the girl's safety to letters, closing the account he has been keeping and preparing, for the first time in nearly twenty years, to leave the valley for good.
suggested_refs: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, on Tampenteire, father of Condwiramurs

segments.name: Dornachbrugg: Condwiramurs Delivered, and the Writing of the Grail

stops.name: Montpellier, the orphaned niece received
stops.campa: Willehalm-Kyot takes his brother's daughter Condwiramurs into his own household at Montpellier, the city he has favored since his years as duke of the Catalan march, and sets himself as her guardian in the same spirit that once carried Sigune to Hohenburg. He is by any ordinary count an old man now, eighty-six years by the chroniclers' abandoned reckoning, yet the tradition shows him still riding, still building, laying out streets and gardens in Montpellier between the hours he gives to the girl's education and to the grail-account still growing at his writing table.
suggested_refs: Montpellier's medieval street plan, traditionally credited in part to Kyot's urban planning
sources: Ellen Schalk, 'Kyot and the Stellar Script of Parsifal' (1987)

stops.name: Montpellier, the years of teaching, word of Parzival
stops.campa: Through the years he keeps her, word comes to Montpellier of a young knight named Parzival, questing far to the north and east, who has by report already once failed at Munsalvaesche and turned from God before turning back. Willehalm-Kyot, who found the same castle by a harder road and married into its keeping, recognizes in the reports the shape of his own old search and begins, the tradition says, to ready Condwiramurs for a meeting he has already started arranging in his mind, the last piece of the grail account he means to close not on paper but in the world.
suggested_refs: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, books IV and V, Parzival's wooing of Condwiramurs

stops.name: Besançon, on the road to Dornachbrugg
stops.campa: In the spring of the year the astronomers of his own school will one day fix past doubt, Willehalm-Kyot leaves Montpellier for the last time with Condwiramurs in his charge, retracing in reverse the road he rode as a young grail-seeker from Provence to the Rhine. He is past ninety by the count the chronicles gave up keeping decades before; the tradition does not trouble itself with the arithmetic, only with the fact of the old man still moving, still delivering what is owed. Through the Burgundian gate at Besançon they pass, then the Jura foothills near Arlesheim where he once found the grail-house itself, and ahead of them both the bridge and town called Dornachbrugg.
suggested_refs: The road from Montpellier through Alsace to the Birs valley near Arlesheim

stops.name: Dornachbrugg, Whitsun, Condwiramurs given to Parzival
stops.campa: On Whitsunday, a date the tradition's own astronomers calculate against the return of Saturn to its house and confirm centuries later against a planetarium, Willehalm-Kyot brings Condwiramurs across the bridge at Dornach and delivers her into Parzival's hands, closing in a single meeting the account of a niece raised, a search completed, and a debt of kinship paid in full. Parzival, newly named king at Munsalvaesche, receives his wife from the hand of the same old man who once found that grail-house by his own hard road. Willehalm-Kyot has now, by any reckoning but the ordinary chronicles', outlived his own recorded death by thirty-six years to stand at this bridge.
stops.quote: dô der sterne Sâturnus / wider an sîn zil gestuont, / daz wart uns bî der wunden kuont
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival 489,24-26 (Saturn's return marking the season of the wound, the reckoning the tradition credits to Kyot-Willehalm)
suggested_refs: The bridge at Dornach over the Birs, near Arlesheim
sources: Wilhelm Deinert, Ritter und Kosmos im Parzival (1960)
Willehalm Institut für Anthroposophie, planetarium verification

stops.name: Montpellier, the return, and the writing that becomes the source
stops.campa: Willehalm-Kyot rides back to Montpellier alone, the office of guardian finished, and takes up for the last time the account he has kept in fragments since Le Verdus: Alischanz and Gyburc, the Arabic manuscript and Flegetanis's starwriting, Munsalvaesche and Schoysiane, Sigune's leash and Condwiramurs's wedding, the whole ninety-year weight of it set down as the true report only its own witness could give. He commits it to an oral transmission that will run through the Provençal courts for three and a half centuries before a German poet named Wolfram finds it and swears, against his own age's doubt, that he says nothing but what his master Kyot has spoken.
stops.quote: Ob von Troys meister Cristjân / disem mære hât unreht getân, / daz mac wol zürnen Kyôt, / der uns diu rehten mære enbôt
suggested_refs: The whole Parzival-Willehalm-Titurel trilogy, transmitted as Wolfram's report of Kyot's own account
sources: Ellen Schalk, 'Kyot and the Stellar Script of Parsifal' (1987)
Werner Greub, Willehalm-Kyot: der Gewährsmann Wolframs von Eschenbach (1991)
